subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Quantal Response Equilibrium
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Quantal Response Equilibrium.

hook.text: A player picks the better option 70% of the time, not 100%. They know which is better but occasionally choose the worse.

buildup.text: Quantal response equilibrium (QRE) models imperfect decision-making. Better options are chosen more often but not.

discovery.text: McKelvey and Palfrey showed QRE explains data better than Nash in many games.

twist.text: As stakes increase, behavior gets closer to Nash. Higher payoffs motivate more careful thinking.

climax.text: QRE teaches a practical lesson: expect opponents to make mistakes, and plan for error, both theirs and yours.

punchline.text: We choose well most of the time. But not all of the time.

quiz.question: What does QRE suggest about decision-making?
options: People always choose the mathematically optimal option
Better options are chosen more often but noise causes occasional errors
People choose randomly regardless of payoffs

details.summary: Quantal response equilibrium replaces the perfect rationality assumption with the idea that players choose better strategies more often but occasionally make mistakes, with the probability of each choice proportional to its expected payoff.
details.whyItMatters: QRE provides a more realistic equilibrium concept that accounts for human error. It explains why dominated strategies are sometimes played and why equilibrium behavior is approximate rather than exact in real strategic settings.
takeaways: Better strategies are chosen more often but not always
Error rates decrease as payoff differences increase
QRE predicts experimental data better than Nash equilibrium in many games

faq.question: How is QRE different from Nash equilibrium?
faq.answer: Nash equilibrium assumes players always choose the best response with certainty. QRE allows for probabilistic mistakes where better responses are chosen more often but not always. As noise decreases, QRE converges to Nash.

faq.question: What does QRE predict that Nash cannot?
faq.answer: QRE predicts positive probabilities for dominated strategies, more cooperative behavior in social dilemmas than Nash predicts, and comparative statics that match observed data better. It captures the noise inherent in human decision-making.
